title: Chapter 83 — Delivery, Install, Haul-Away & Accessories
intro: The service lines as products, the operational handshake, and accessory discipline.

sections.title: Delivery as a Product
sections.content:
Delivery is not logistics. It is a product you are selling. The customer is paying for two people to bring a heavy appliance into their home, navigate stairs and doorways, place it in position, and make it work. That is a skilled service.

Present it that way: 'Our delivery includes a two-person team, in-home placement, connection to your existing hookups, and a full operational test before they leave. They will also remove all packaging.'

sections.title: Installation Requirements by Category
sections.content:
Every appliance has requirements that must be verified BEFORE the sale, not discovered at delivery.

Refrigeration: measure the opening width, height, depth. Measure the delivery path — a 36-inch fridge does not fit through a 32-inch doorway. Check water line for ice maker.

Cooking: verify fuel source and line capacity. A 48-inch pro range may need a 3/4-inch gas line. Electric ranges need 240V/40A or 50A. Anti-tip bracket is required by code for all freestanding ranges.

Laundry: hot and cold water supply, drain, gas or 240V electric for dryer. Check venting path for exterior exhaust. Verify stacking kit compatibility.

Dishwashers: 24-inch opening standard. Measure under-counter height including countertop thickness. Verify water supply, drain, and electrical connections.

Always document the customer's measurements on the quote. A $50 measurement appointment prevents a $500 return.

sections.title: Accessories That Sell
sections.content:
Stacking kits for laundry — $25-50 each. Pedestals — $250-400 each and high margin. Water filters for fridges — recurring revenue. Range accessories — griddle plates, wok grates. Vent hood accessories — charcoal filters for recirculating, duct kits.

Present accessories at quote time. They convert far better in the quote than as an afterthought at pickup.
